In my town, when someone is about to disappear, their shoes walk home first.
A pair of shoes comes walking up the street.
They climb onto a porch and stop.
At midnight, the owner is gone.
All that's left are bare footprints in the snow, walking into the woods.
The chapel board counts us every morning.
My little brother Max is eight, and he wears my old sneakers.
When I gave them to him, I said, "What's mine is yours."
He never stopped saying it back.
Grandma watched him lace them up and said,
"Shoes don't care whose feet they're on."
The first night, Mrs Ruiz's slippers came home.
She put them on to see if they still fit.
Bare footprints, right into the trees.
Then old Mr Hale's boots came home.
He laughed, pulled them on and went out to shovel his porch.
Just a shovel, standing in the snow.
Then baby Lily's tiny shoes came home.
Her mom grabbed them and hid them in the closet, so Lily would never see them.
At midnight, her mom was gone.
But Lily was still asleep in her crib.
Strangely, the footprints outside were big.
The whole town said her mom went looking for her.
Mr Ortiz sold hot cocoa to everyone watching the woods.
Max's sneakers walked up our porch steps.
I couldn't let him touch them.
So I picked them up myself, ran them out to the woods and threw them as hard as I could.
They were back on the porch.
Max was shaking under his blanket.
I shoved them inside my own boots, under my bed, and sat on top of it all.
That's when I noticed my socks.
Wet with snow I never walked in.
I hugged him and laughed so hard I cried.
Shoes don't care whose feet they're on.
The next night, a pair of boots walked up our porch.
